ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, to make the voltage U equal to 2 V, what is the value of the resistor R (Ω)?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure is an ideal 4 V voltage source, marked with the upper end as positive and the lower end as negative, connected between the upper and lower common rails. The middle branch has a 10 Ω resistor, also connected between the same pair of upper and lower rails. In the right branch, the upper part is a 2 Ω resistor, and the lower part is an unknown resistor R, the two are in series; the voltage U is marked across R, with the positive end above R and the negative end below R. Then reason: the ideal 4 V voltage source fixes the voltage between the upper and lower rails at 4 V. The middle 10 Ω resistor is only in parallel with the power source and the right branch, and does not change the total 4 V voltage across the right branch. In the right branch, 2 Ω and R are in series, so the voltage on R is given by the voltage division formula: U = 4 × R/(R + 2). It is required that U = 2 V, therefore 2 = 4R/(R + 2). Solving gives 2(R + 2) = 4R, that is 2R + 4 = 4R, so R = 2 Ω.
